query: Equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni and its quaternary and ternary subsets provide 16 candidate alloys, nine of which are single-phase FCC after thermomechanical processing. Early reports associated increasing constituent count with greater strength, but that simple relationship is no longer generally accepted. Despite extensive experimental and theoretical investigation, the origins of differences in deformation and failure behavior remain unresolved; practical interpretation must also account for constituent cost and overall cost-performance balance. What testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs these mechanical-property differences and why? Define a controlled investigation, the observations predicted relative to the equiatomic quinary baseline, the limits within which the hypothesis should apply, the prior evidence supporting it, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In single‐phase FCC high-entropy alloys, variations in mechanical properties among equiatomic, quaternary, and ternary alloys result from differences in local lattice distortion that alter stacking fault energies (SFE) and promote different degrees of short-range chemical order. These local structural differences modulate dislocation mobility and slip behavior, thereby governing strength and ductility.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni alloy processed to form a single-phase FCC structure via identical thermomechanical routes.
generation.intervention: Systematic compositional modification to form quaternary and ternary subsets from the equiatomic baseline while keeping processing conditions constant.
generation.conditions: All alloys are synthesized to obtain single-phase FCC structures via identical thermomechanical processing. Mechanical testing (tensile, nanoindentation) and microstructural characterization (TEM, XRD, atom probe tomography) are performed at room and elevated temperatures under controlled strain rates.
generation.structural_mediator: Local lattice distortions that alter the stacking fault energy and enable different degrees of chemical short-range order.
generation.mechanism: Compositional changes modify the effective atomic volume mismatch, leading to spatial fluctuations in lattice parameters. These fluctuations change the stacking fault energy locally, which in turn affects dislocation nucleation, mobility, and slip system activation. The cumulative effect is a shift in the balance between strength and ductility relative to the quinary baseline.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni baseline, quaternary and ternary alloys with increased atomic mismatch will show higher strength and hardness due to enhanced lattice distortion and solid-solution strengthening, but may exhibit reduced ductility because of constrained dislocation motion. The trend should correlate with measured stacking fault energies and local lattice distortions.
generation.baseline: Equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni alloy with single-phase FCC structure prepared under identical thermomechanical processing conditions.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to apply only in single-phase FCC HEAs produced by thermomechanical processing. It may not hold in multiphase alloys or in systems where grain-boundary effects or other processing-induced defects dominate the mechanical response.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty whether additional microstructural features such as grain-boundary character, nano-precipitates, or dislocation substructures might also significantly influence the observed mechanical properties. The interplay of these factors with local lattice distortion could complicate the isolation of the proposed mechanism.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of FCC alloys: the equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni baseline and its controlled quaternary and ternary derivatives. Under identical thermomechanical processing, conduct a coordinated microstructural and mechanical property evaluation. Measure local lattice distortions (via high-resolution XRD and TEM), stacking fault energies (using in situ TEM techniques and instrumented indentation), and dislocation dynamics. Correlate these measurements with tensile and hardness tests.
measurements: Quantitative lattice distortion from XRD peak broadening and TEM imaging
Stacking fault energy measurements via in situ TEM or indentation techniques
Dislocation density and mobility through TEM observations during deformation
Mechanical property data from tensile tests and nanoindentation
Assessment of chemical short-range order via atom probe tomography
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the measured variations in local lattice distortion and stacking fault energy do not correlate with the differences in mechanical properties—as predicted (i.e., increased lattice distortion and lower SFE should lead to higher strength and hardness with reduced ductility)—then the hypothesis would be considered falsified.
